la:verb:emergo.html:
ē-mergo, si, sum, 3, v. a. and n.
Act., to bring forth, bring to light, raise up (very rare; mostly with se, or pass. in mid. sense), to come forth, come out, to rise up, emerge (not in Plaut., Caes., Verg., or Hor.).
Lit.: emersere e gurgite vultus Nereides,: ex undis Cancri pars sese emergit in astra,; se torrens imo hiatu,: se lux pelago,: tibi (somnianti) subito sum visus emersus e flumine,; so, emersus e palude,: emersus paludibus,.— Poet.: cernis et emersas in lucem tendere noctes,; nox emersa,.—
Trop., to extricate or free one's self, to raise one's self up, to rise: sese ex malis, Ruhnk.; so : homo emersus subito ex diuturnis tenebris lustrorum ac stuprorum,; cf.: tu emersus e caeno,: velut emerso ab admiratione animo,—Once perh. act.: ut possim rerum tantas emergere moles,.—Far more freq. and class.,
Neutr. (i. q. the preceding emergere se), to come forth, come up, arise, emerge.
Lit.
In gen.: equus emersit e flumine,: e vadis,: ex alto,: de paludibus,: ab infima ara (anguis),: sub exsistentibus glebis (pisces),: extra aquam ; : foras (with exsilire),: ad ortus,: in suam lucem (luna), et saep.: ex Antiati in Appiam ad Tres Tabernas,to get away, escape,; cf.: e patrio regno (with Cappadociae latebris se occultare),: aegre in apertos campos (Manlius),—Absol.: aves, quae se in mari mergerent: quae cum emersissent, etc.,; cf. : sol. (also, ); ; cf. stellae,—Impers. tot res repente circumvallant, unde emergi non potest, .—
In partic., to come forth, come up, break forth, as a plant or animal, when it springs up or is born: viriditas e vaginis emergit, etc.,; cf.: flos ex caule,: totus infans utero,: ova,: ventus,.—
Trop., to extricate one's self from, to raise one's self up, to emerge, get clear: ex sermone emersit,: ex miserrimis naturae tuae sordibus,: ex peculatus judicio,: ex paternis probris ac vitiis,: ex mendicitate,: vixdum e naufragiis prioris culpae cladisque,: ex obnoxia pace,: ex omni saevitia fortunae (virtus),; : cum tam multa ex illo mari (sc. Ponto) bella emerserint, have arisen,

broken out, : equidem multos vidi emersisse aliquando, et se ad frugem bonam, ut dicitur, recepisse,have raised themselves up, have risen,: hac autem re incredibile est quantum civitates emerserint,have raised themselves up, elevated themselves,; cf.: ad summas opes,; : in quod fastigium,; : quamvis enim demersae sint leges, emergunt tamen haec aliquando,; cf. : nunc emergit amor,; cf. dolor,: ex quo magis emergit, quale sit decorum illud, etc.,appears, is evident,; cf.: tanti sceleris indicium per Fulviam emersit,.
la:verb:emergo.inflection: si, sum, 3, v. a. and n.

la:noun:emptio.gloss: the act of buying or purchasing, purchase
senses: the act of buying or purchasing, purchase
la:noun:emptio.html:
emptĭo (emt-), ōnis, f.
id.
,
a buying, purchase (cf.: sectio, mercatura, etc.).
Prop., ; ; ; ; ; et saep.; cf., on its legal relations,; the title: De emptione et venditione,; ; and Rein's Privatr. p. 329 sq.: equina, i. e. of horses (with boum and asinorum), .—
Transf.
A purchase, i. e. an article purchased: ex illis emptionibus nullam desidero,; .—
A purchase-deed, bill of sale,

la:verb:emo.html:
ĕmo, ēmi, emptum, 3 (
perf. subj. emissim, ), v. a.
the same word with EMERE=accipere, Paul. ex Fest. pp. 4, 18, and 76, 1 Müll.; cf. adimo and demo; prop., to take; root yam; Sanscr. yamati, hold fast, Fick, Vergl. Wört. p. 158 sq.; cf. note
, to buy, purchase (very freq. in all periods and kinds of composition).
Lit.: is postquam hunc emit, dedit eum, etc.,: qui puellam ab eo emerat,: emit hosce de praeda,; ; : aliquid de aliquo,; ; ; .—With gen. or abl. pretii (cf. Zumpt, Gram. § 444): Ep. Quanti eam emit? Th. Vili. Ep. Quot minis? Th. Quadraginta minis, ; so, quanti,: tanti, quanti, etc.,: minoris aut pluris,; ; : duodeviginti minis,: duobus milibus nummum,: magno, parvo,: immenso quaedam,: bene,i. e. cheap,; : male,i. e. dear,; cf. care,: quatuor tabernas in publicum,for the public,; fin.: piper in libras,by the pound,: fundum in diem,on time, on credit,: per assem et libram,i. e. to adopt,—Perf. part. pass. as subst.
empta, ae, f., she who is bought, the slave, .—
emptum, i, n., the purchase, contract of purchase: quae ex empto aut vendito aut conducto aut locato contra fidem fiunt,through buying and selling,; so in jurid. lang.: ex empto,; cf. the title: De actionibus empti et venditi,; .— Prov.: emere oportet, quem oboedire velis tibi,.—
Trop., to buy, buy up, to purchase, gain, acquire, procure, obtain: aliquando desinat ea se putare posse emere, quae ipse semper habuit venalia, fidem, jusjurandum, etc.,; cf.: sententias (judicum),; and: animos centurionum,: ex his (tribunis plebis) emitur ab inimicis meis is, quem, etc.,: militem,; : exercitum,: percussorem in aliquem, et saep.: aliquem beneficiis,to gain over,; cf. : aliquem dote,: spem pretio,: immortalitatem morte,; cf.: aeternum nomen sanguine,: pulmenta laboribus,: voluptatem dolore, et saep.—With a clause as object, : furtis in manibus emptum est Oedipodae sedisse loco,: quantine emptum velit Hannibal, ut nos Vertentes terga aspiciat?; .

la:verb:emereo.gloss: to earn, merit, gain by service
senses: to earn, merit, gain by service
to serve out; to serve one's time; to complete one's obligation to serve
la:verb:emereo.html:
ē-mĕrĕo, ŭi, ĭtum, 2, v. a., and (perh. not ante-Aug.) ē-mĕrĕor, ĭtus, 2,
v. dep. a.
To obtain by service, to gain, earn, merit, deserve.
In gen. (rare; not in Cic.): quid ego emerui mali?: honores,mihi altior sollicitudo, quale judicium hominum, emererer, accessit,; cf.: emerendi favoris gratia canunt,: pecuniam ex eo quaestu uberem, Gell, 6, 7, 5.—Poet., with inf. clause as object: Ennius emeruit Contiguus poni, Scipio magne, tibi,; cf. .—Pass., in the part. perf.: emerito caput insere caelo,; so ; .—
In Tib. and Ov. emerere aliquem, like demereri aliquem, to gain the favor of any one, to deserve well of, to lay under obligation: viros,; ; ; .—Far more frequent,
To serve out, complete one's term of service.
Prop., in milit. lang.: spes emerendi stipendia,; in part. perf.: emerita stipendia, Kritz.; ; ; : militia,: arma,: anni,; cf. .—As a v. dep.: stipendia emeritus,.—Hence, subst.ēmĕrĭ-tus, i, m., a soldier who has served out his time, a veteran, an exempt, ; ; —
Transf. beyond the milit. sphere: annuum tempus (sc. magistratus) emeritum habere,; cf.: annuae operae emerentur,: spatium juventae (homo) transit, et emeritis medii quoque temporis annis, etc.,.—In part. perf.: emeritus, a, um (since the Aug. per. in the mid. signif.), that has become unfit for service, worn out: equi,; cf.: apes fessae et jam emeritae,; so, palmes,: aratrum,: latus (with invalidum),: acus,: rogus,i. e. burned out, extinguished,
la:verb:emereo.inflection: ŭi, ĭtum, 2, v. a., ĭtus, 2, v. dep. a.

la:noun:emptor.html:
emptor (emt-), ōris, m.
id.
,
a buyer, purchaser (cf.: negotiator, mercator, caupo, institor),; ; ; ; ; ; et saep.; cf., on the laws affecting him, the authorities cited under emptio: pretiosus dedecorum, i. e. who buys them dearly (=magno pretio emens), : familiae, the imaginary purchaser of an inheritance per aes et libram, Bremi; cf. Rein's Privatr. p. 375.

la:verb:emendo.gloss: to free from faults, correct, improve, remedy, amend, revise, cure
senses: to free from faults, correct, improve, remedy, amend, revise, cure
to correct by punishment, chastise, atone or compensate for
la:verb:emendo.html:
ē-mendo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
mendum
,
to free from faults, to correct, improve, amend (cf. corrigo—class.; not in Caes.): tota civitas emendari et corrigi solet continentia principum,; cf. ; ; : leviter tuum consilium (with conformare),: consuetudinem vitiosam,: vitia adolescentiae multis virtutibus,: facta priora novis,: res Italas legibus,: legem severius,: sucos acerbos in pomis,; cf. terram terrā,: bovem cubitorem fame et siti,: angorem animi (sui),.—Esp. freq. of correcting, emending language (oral or written), ; ; ; et saep.—In medic. lang., like corrigere, for to cure: alopecias,: tussim,: albugines oculorum,: cicatrices, et saep. —
In post-class. lang. in partic., to correct by punishment, to chastise: libertum non obsequentem aut verbis aut fustium castigatione,; ; — Hence, ēmendātus, a, um, P. a., faultless, perfect, pure: mores,; cf. vir,; : e. et Latina locutio,; cf. ; ; : opus,: aquae,.—Comp.: mulier,: vita,.— Sup.: homo (with optimus),: libri, Quint. Ep. ad Tryph. § 3; cf.: correcta et emendata maxime,.—Adv.: ēmendāte, faultlessly, perfectly, purely: loqui, scribere, etc.,; ; ; prooem. § 6; .—Comp.: facere capillum,; Zumpt.

la:verb:emorior.html:
ē-mŏrĭor, mortuus, 3 (old form of the
inf. emoriri, ; but , moriri, Ritschl), v. dep. n., to die off, to die, depart, decease, v. Doed. Syn. 3, p. 183 sq. (freq. and class.).
Lit.: emori me malim,; so ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; .—Prov.: verba facit emortuo, he talks to the dead, i. e. in vain, .—
Transf., of things, to become dead, to die: membrum,: arbor,; : carbo,i. e. to go out,: sterilis et emoriens terra,desert,; cf. vulva,.—
Trop., to perish, pass away, cease: quorum laus emori non potest,: vis,: dicta (with evanescere),: spes

(opp. elucere), : amor,: auxilium,.

senses: to spring out, spring forth, to break forth
la:verb:emico.html:
ē-mĭco, cŭi (cf. ), cātum, 1, v. n.,
to spring out, spring forth, to break forth, appear quickly (not freq. till after the Aug. per.; in Cic. and Caes. not at all).
Lit.: emicat ex oculis, spirat quoque pectore flamma,: flamma ex monte,: multi calami ex una radice,: dracones de extis,: fulgura ab omni parte caeli,: corpore sanguis (so Lachm.; Munro, e corpore),: uterque pronus carcere,: scaturigines,: cruor alte,: sanguis per foramen,: scintillae inter fumum,: sol super terras,; cf. dies,: telum nervo,; cf.: saxa tormento,: hostem rati, emicant, sine discrimine insultant, rushforth, et saep.: (sanguis) in illam partem,: juvenum manus emicat ardens in litus,; cf.: in currum,: Nisus ante omnia corpora,: sanguis in altum,: rami in excelsum,; cf. comically: cor coepit in pectus emicare, to leap, * .—
Transf., to stretch forth, project: scopulus alto gurgite,.—
Trop., to be prominent or conspicuous, to become apparent: inter quae verbum emicuit si forte decorum,: Agrippinae is pavor, ea consternatio mentis emicuit, ut, etc.,.—Esp. of good qualities, etc.: quos et magnitudine animi et claritate rerum longe emicuisse,to have shone forth,: egregia virtus Scaevae centurionis emicuit,; cf.: inter ceteros Themistoclis gloria emicuit,.

senses: to let forth, let go, send out
la:verb:emitto.html:
ē-mitto, mīsi, missum, 3, v. a.,
to send out, send forth, to let out, let go (freq. and class.).
Lit.
In gen.: quibuscum tamquam e carceribus emissus sis,; cf.: aperiam carceres et equos emittere incipiam,: ex porta ludis cum emissu'st lepus,: aliquem e carcere,: aliquem ex vinculis,; : aliquem e custodia, (cf. ).—As milit. t. t., to send out against the enemy: essedarios ex silvis,; cf.: equitibus emissis,: Caesar omnibus portis eruptione facta equitatuque emisso hostes in fugam dat,; 5, 58, 4 et saep.: aliquem de carcere,; cf.: Licinium fugere conantem de manibus,; ; for which: Hannibalem e manibus,; and merely manibus,: aliquem noctu per vallum,: aliquem pabulatum,; cf. : aliquem sub jugum, et saep.: ut abs te non emissus ex urbe, sed immissus in urbem esse videatur,sent out, turned out,; cf. : scutum manu,to throw away, throw aside,: pila,to throw, hurl, cast, discharge,; ; et saep.; cf.: hastam in fines eorum,: aquam ex lacu Albano,to let off,; cf.: aquam impetu,: lacus Velinus, a Curio emissus,; : flumen per prona montis,: sanguinem de aure,to let,; cf.: sanguinem venis,: ova,to lay,: folia,to put forth, produce,; cf. transf.: ulmi emittuntur in ramos,: librum de arte aleam ludendi,to put forth, publish,; cf.: aliquid dignum nostro nomine emittere,: fulmina,: sonitum ex alto,; cf.: vocem caelo,: sonitum linguae,: vocem,to utter,; ; et saep.: flatum crepitumque ventris,: animam, to expire, Nep. Epam. 9, 3: spiritum,: si nubium conflictu ardor expressus se emiserit, id esse fulmen,has broken forth, burst forth,.—
In partic.: manu emittere aliquem for the usu. manu mittere aliquem, to release a person from one's potestas, to set free, emancipate (anteclass. and since the Aug. per.), ; ; et saep.; ; ; ; ; ; so without manu,; ; cf. of a debtor: libra et aere liberatum emittit,.
Trop., to let forth, let go, send out: manibus manifesta suis emittere quoquam,to let slip from our hands that which is evident,; cf.: emissa de manibus res est,: cum illud facetum dictum emissum haerere debeat (a fig. borrowed from missive weapons),; cf.: et semel emissum volat irrevocabile verbum,: argumenta,; and: maledictum,

la:verb:emunio.gloss: to fortify, strengthen, defend (with a wall)
senses: to fortify, strengthen, defend (with a wall)
la:verb:emunio.html:
ē-mūnĭo, īvi or ii, ītum, 4, v. a.,
to fortify, secure, provide with a wall (not ante-Aug.).
Lit.: locum arcis in modum,: non opus est arduos colles emunire,.—
Transf.
To strengthen, make secure: obice postes,: murum opere,: caveam retibus,: sola et latera horreorum,.—
To protect, defend: vites caveis ab injuria pecoris,.—
To build up, elevate for defence: murus, ut in suspecto loco, supra ceterae modum altitudinis, emunitus erat,. 7, 7: locus in modum arcis emunitus,.—
To pile up, heap up: toros ostro auroque,.—(ε) To clear, to make passable: silvas ac paludes,.—
Trop.: emunivit animum, Bip.
la:verb:emunio.inflection: īvi or ii, ītum, 4, v. a.

senses: to be prominent, stand out in relief
to be or become conspicuous or prominent, stand out (through one's good qualities); to be eminent, excel
la:verb:emineo.html:
ē-mĭnĕo, ŭi, 2, v. n.,
to stand out, project (freq. and class.).
Lit.
In gen. (syn.: exstare, excedere): cum ex terra nihil emineret, quod contemplationi caeli officere posset,: globus terrae e mari,: stipites ex terra,; cf.: stipites ab ramis, § 3: belua ponto,: rupes aequore,: moles aquā,: oculi extra terram,: balaena dorso multum super aquas,: super corpus quasi verrucula,: ferrum per costas, et saep.—Absol., ; ; ; et saep.; cf. alte,: hasta in partes ambas,: jugum in mare,; cf.: lingua in altum (i. e. mare),.—
In partic., in painting, to stand out in relief, be prominent, as the lights in a picture, ; ; ; ; cf. eminentia, I.—
Trop., to be prominent, stand out, become conspicuous (syn.: eluceo, praecello, excello, appareo, praesto, antecedo).
In gen.: animus, cum erit inclusus in corpore, eminebit foras,will extend beyond, Mos.: ii quorum eminet audacia atque projecta est,: quod quo studiosius ab ipsis opprimitur et absconditur, eo magis eminet et apparet,comes out, becomes visible,; cf. Zumpt N. cr.; ; ; ; Spald.; ; ; ; ; : vix ex gratulando miser jam eminebam,was but now emerging from the flood of congratulations,: vox eminet una,makes itself distinctly audible,.—
In partic., to be prominent, conspicuous through one's (good) qualities, to distinguish one's self, be eminent: Demosthenes unus eminet inter omnes in omni genere dicendi,; so with inter, ; ; cf. with super, : in aliqua re,; ; : aliqua re,; ; ; .—Absol.: excellit atque eminet vis, potestas, etc.,; so with excellit,: quae (sententiarum ornamenta) emineant pauciora,; so ; : altius,.—Hence, ēmĭnens, entis, P. a., standing out, projecting, prominent, high, lofty.
Lit. (syn. editus): promontoria,: trabes,: saxa,: oculi,: genae leviter,: statura,: capita papaverum,; : aedes, standing on high ground (opp. plana), : nihil (in globo),; cf. ; cf. also the art. eminentia: patibulo eminens affigebatur, Fragm. ap. (4, 40 Dietsch).—Comp.: trabes,: nasus a summo,; of perspective in painting: alia eminentiora, alia reductiora fecerunt,.—Sup.: aliquod in montibus (i. e. vertex),; cf. mons,.—
Trop., lofty, distinguished, eminent (esp. freq. in the postAug. per., and mostly in the sup.; syn.: praeclarus, praestans, excellens, etc.): species deorum quae nihil solidi habeat, nihil eminentis,: ingenium,: res dictu,.—Prov.: eminentis fortunae comes invidia,.—Plur. as subst.: ēmĭnentes, ĭum, m., distinguished men, .—ēmĭnentĭa, ĭum, n.
Admirable passages in an oration, .—
Greatness, distinction: nun. quam eminentia invidia carent,.—Comp.: eloquentia,.—Sup.: auctores,; ; ; 9, 4, 79 et saep.; cf. Ruhnk. — In the later empire, Eminentissimus was a title of the Praefectus praetorio, and of the Magister militum, ; et saep.—Adv.: ēmĭnenter, highly, eminently, .— Comp.: projectae cautes eminentius,: non eminentius quam municipaliter natus,i. e. of higher, nobler birth,.

la:adv:eminus.html:
ē-mĭnus, adv.
manus; cf. the opp. comminus; lit., hands apart, i. e. not hand to hand
,
aloof, at fighting distance with missiles, a spear's-throw off (cf.: longe, procul).
Prop., a milit. t. t., used of fighting with missiles, spears, etc. (class.), mostly opp. comminus: eminus fundis, sagittis reliquisque telis pugnabatur,. 1; cf. ; ; ; ; ; ; ; saep.; of throwing fire, etc.: alii faces de muro in aggerem eminus jaciebant,.—
Transf., in gen., at a distance, from a distance (mostly postAug.): oppugnationem eminus incipere,: fer opem eminus unam, Ov.

P. 1, 6, 17; ; ; .

senses: to pass through or over, traverse
la:verb:emetior.html:
ē-mētĭor, mensus, 4,
v. dep. a., to measure out (not freq. till after the Aug. per.).
Lit.: spatium oculis,: longitudines et altitudines vocis,.—
Transf.
To pass through, pass over, traverse a certain space: cum freta, cum terras omnis, tot inhospita saxa Sideraque emensae ferimur,; ; ; ; ; fin.; ; ; ; cf. poet.: pelagi terraeque laborem,; and in Tacitus, of time: Galba quinque principes prosperā fortunā emensus,i. e. having survived,.—
To impart, beslow: non aliquid patriae tanto emetiris acervo? * : ego voluntatem tibi profecto emetior, sed rem ipsam nondum posse videor, * .!*? ēmensus, a, um, Part. in pass. signif. (acc. to II. A. and B.).
Passed through, traversed: multo major pars itineris,; so ; ; ; .—
Imparted, distributed, .

emendo

la:verb:emigro.gloss: to depart from somewhere, emigrate, move out
senses: to depart from somewhere, emigrate, move out
la:verb:emigro.html:
ē-mī^gro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.
Neutr., to remove, depart from a place, to emigrate (rare but classical): Se. Quid tu ais? num hinc emigrasti? Me. Quem in locum? etc., ; cf. ; : ex illa domo,: domo,; .—Trop.: e vita,.—Absol.: in hasce aedis pedem nemo intro tetulit, semel ut emigravimus,; : qui post hunc casum emigraverunt,.—
Act. (only ante- and postclass.).
To remove: senia et jurgia sesemet aedibus emigrarunt, Titin. ap. (Com. v. 148 Rib.): emigrabit te tabernaculo suo,.—*
Scripturas, to transgress, .

ēmissĭo, ōnis, f.
id.
,

Prop., a letting go: radiorum ex oculis,a darting forth,: mortui sunt in emissione,in exile,.—*

la:verb:emano.gloss: to flow out; arise or emanate (from)
senses: to flow out; arise or emanate (from)
la:verb:emano.html:
ē-māno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n.,
to flow out (class.; esp. freq. in the trop. signif. and in Cic.).
Lit., ; Cic. poët. Div. 2, 30; ; —
Trop.
To spring out of, to arise, proceed, emanate from: alii quoque allo ex fonte praeceptores dicendi emanaverunt,; cf. : ex quo (loco) vis omnis oportet emanet ratiocinationis,; cf. : hinc haec recentior Academia emanavit,fin.: istinc mala,: singularem eloquii suavitatem ore ejus emanaturam,ext.—
To spread itself, be diffused: emanabat latius malum,.—Esp. freq.,
In partic., of things that are made public, to spread abroad, become known: oratio in vulgus emanare poterit,; cf. ; ; ; ; ; Cael. ap. ; ; ; et saep.; cf. with a subject acc. and inf.: multis emanabat indiciis fratrem Volscii ne assurrexisse quidem ex morbo,; .

la:noun:eminentia.html:
ēmĭnentĭa, ae, f.
eminens
,
a standing out, projecting; concr., a prominence, protuberance.
Lit., (with soliditas); no. 18, p. 359; and in plur., . —Hence, in painting, the prominent, i. e. light parts, (opp. umbrae). —
Trop., excellence: quaedam formarum,: senectutis suae,.—Hence, per eminentiam, i. q. κατʼ ἐξοχήν, preëminently, par excellence, : reperiet, eminentiam cujusque operis artissimis temporum claustris circumdatam, the highest ability in an art, .

emptīcĭus (emt-) or -tĭus, a, um, adj.
emo

la:verb:emundo.html:
ē-mundo, no
perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to clean out, make quite clean (a favorite word of Columella; not in , where the right reading is emendat): bubilia,; cf. ; : humum,: pennas gallinae,: vinum,to purify,; cf. segetes,—
Trop., to cleanse, purify from sin (eccl. Lat.): conscientiam nostram, et saep.

la:verb:emancipo.html:
ē-mancĭpo (ēmancŭpo), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.—Jurid. t. t.
In the strict sense, to put out of the hand and power of the paterfamilias; to declare free and independent, to emancipate a son from the patria potestas by the thrice-repeated act of mancipatio and manumissio, ; ; ; ; et saep.; cf. Sandars, introd. p. 37 sq.—
In a wider sense, to give from under one's own power or authority into that of another.
Prop.: filium in adoptionem,; cf. , and Paul. ex Müll.: agrum,; cf.: praedia paterna, Quint. 6, 3, 44.—
Transf. beyond the jurid. sphere, to give up, surrender, sell: mulier, tibi me emancupo: tuus sum,; cf. : (senectus) si jus suum retinet, si nemini emancipata est,; cf.: venditus atque emancipatus tribunatus,.

la:noun:emolumentum.html:
ēmŏlŭmentum or ēmŏlĭmentum (cf. monumentum), i, n.
emolior; lit., a working out; hence
,
A striving for success, i. e. effort, exertion, labor (cf. elaboro; rarely): neque enim magnum emolumentum esse potest,can present no great difficulty, (but in , the true reading is molimento). —*
Concr., a work, a building, etc.: vetera, Cod. Th. 15, 1, 19.—Far more freq.,
The attainment of success, i. e. gain, profit, advantage, benefit (syn.: lucrum, quaestus, compendium, commodum, fructus, reditus).
Absol.: et emolumenta et detrimenta (quae ὠφελήματα et βλάμματα appellant) communia esse voluerunt, ; so opp. detrimentum,; cf. opp. damnum,: nullum emolumentum esse, nullum injustitia partum praemium tantum, ut, etc.,; so with praemium,; cf. with utilitas,fin.: boni nullo emolumento impelluntur in fraudem,; cf. ; ; ; ; ; ; ; * et saep.; of persons: ut quam maximum emolumentum novis sociis esset,.—
With gen.: emolumenta rerum fallacibus judiciis vident ... poenam non vident,: victoriae,: belli,; : pacis,: ergastulorum,: laborum,: sacramentorum (with praemia), et saep.: honoris,.

la:verb:emereor.gloss: to earn, merit, gain by service
la:verb:emereor.html:
ē-mĕrĕo, ŭi, ĭtum, 2, v. a., and (perh. not ante-Aug.) ē-mĕrĕor, ĭtus, 2,
v. dep. a.
To obtain by service, to gain, earn, merit, deserve.
In gen. (rare; not in Cic.): quid ego emerui mali?: honores,mihi altior sollicitudo, quale judicium hominum, emererer, accessit,; cf.: emerendi favoris gratia canunt,: pecuniam ex eo quaestu uberem, Gell, 6, 7, 5.—Poet., with inf. clause as object: Ennius emeruit Contiguus poni, Scipio magne, tibi,; cf. .—Pass., in the part. perf.: emerito caput insere caelo,; so ; .—
In Tib. and Ov. emerere aliquem, like demereri aliquem, to gain the favor of any one, to deserve well of, to lay under obligation: viros,; ; ; .—Far more frequent,
To serve out, complete one's term of service.
Prop., in milit. lang.: spes emerendi stipendia,; in part. perf.: emerita stipendia, Kritz.; ; ; : militia,: arma,: anni,; cf. .—As a v. dep.: stipendia emeritus,.—Hence, subst.ēmĕrĭ-tus, i, m., a soldier who has served out his time, a veteran, an exempt, ; ; —
Transf. beyond the milit. sphere: annuum tempus (sc. magistratus) emeritum habere,; cf.: annuae operae emerentur,: spatium juventae (homo) transit, et emeritis medii quoque temporis annis, etc.,.—In part. perf.: emeritus, a, um (since the Aug. per. in the mid. signif.), that has become unfit for service, worn out: equi,; cf.: apes fessae et jam emeritae,; so, palmes,: aratrum,: latus (with invalidum),: acus,: rogus,i. e. burned out, extinguished,
